article.title: Why Customer Retention and Purchase Frequency Measure Different Things

paragraphs.en:
Retention and purchase frequency are often discussed together because both describe customer relationships. However, they answer different questions. Retention asks whether a customer remains active or present over time. Frequency asks how often that customer uses the service or buys from the business. A company can have strong retention while customer activity is quietly weakening.

Consider a supermarket loyalty program. Suppose 90 percent of last year's members still make at least one purchase this year. Retention looks excellent. But imagine that those retained customers used to shop six times per month and now shop only four times. The business has kept the customers according to its retention definition, yet the intensity of the relationship has fallen substantially.

The opposite pattern is also possible. A company may lose many low-frequency customers while its remaining customers visit more often. Overall retention falls, but average frequency among retained customers rises. If management sees only the higher frequency, it may conclude that engagement improved, even though the customer base became smaller.

Definitions matter. A retained customer might mean someone with any transaction in the following year, someone active in each quarter, or someone who has not crossed a formal churn threshold. These definitions produce different retention rates. Frequency also depends on whether analysts count transactions, shopping days, active months, or visits. The metric should match the business behavior being studied.

A useful analysis separates extensive and intensive margins. The extensive margin describes whether customers participate at all: retained versus lost, active versus inactive. The intensive margin describes how much participating customers do: how often they visit, how much they spend, or how many products they use. Looking at both prevents one dimension from hiding deterioration in the other.

Cohort analysis is especially helpful. Start with customers active in a defined base period, then follow the same cohort over time. Report the share still active and, among those retained, the distribution of purchase frequency. Median frequency can be useful because a small group of extremely frequent shoppers may raise the average.

Businesses should also examine transitions. Customers rarely move directly from highly engaged to permanently churned in one step. Frequency may fall from six visits to four, then to two, before activity disappears. A declining-frequency segment can therefore serve as an early-warning group, although any intervention should be evaluated rather than assumed to work.

Seasonality can complicate interpretation. A customer shopping less in February than December may be behaving normally. Comparisons should use equivalent periods or adjust for seasonal patterns. Changes in store availability, pricing, promotions, or household circumstances can also affect frequency without changing the customer's underlying preference.

For reporting, a compact dashboard can show retention rate, retained-customer count, average and median frequency among retained customers, and total transactions. Segmenting by prior frequency level makes the picture more actionable. High-frequency customers who decline slightly may still contribute more than low-frequency customers who remain stable.

The main lesson is simple: staying is not the same as using. Retention tells us whether the relationship continues under a chosen definition. Frequency tells us how intensely the relationship is being used. When both are tracked, analysts can distinguish customer loss from declining engagement and design responses for the actual problem rather than for a misleading summary metric.

article.zh: Retention 衡量客戶是否留下，frequency 衡量留下的人使用多頻繁。兩者需同時看，才能區分流失與關係弱化。
article.ja: 継続率は顧客が残っているか、利用頻度は残った顧客がどれだけ使っているかを表し、別々に確認する必要があります。
business: Are customers leaving, or are retained customers using us less?
Let's track retention and frequency separately.
